conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You came in today because your dialysis access in the left arm stopped working, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doc. At my last session, they couldn’t get it to work. But I didn’t feel any pain or anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We checked with an ultrasound, and it showed a clot in your graft. That’s why it wasn’t working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A clot? Like a blood clot? Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it blocks the access. But we’ve placed a temporary catheter in your groin so you can still get dialysis. That’s already done, and you’re all set for tonight’s session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I didn’t even feel that. But will the clot go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We plan to remove it tomorrow with a procedure called a thrombectomy. It’s done by a specialist using imaging to guide tools into the graft and clear the clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some medication to keep you comfortable. You’ll be awake but relaxed. Most patients feel only pressure, not pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my potassium was high earlier, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was very high, which can be dangerous for the heart. But we gave you some treatments, and you’ve already had two hours of dialysis. Your levels are much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had that before. My feet are bothering me again though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know your neuropathy pain can be tough. We’ll keep your gabapentin and oxycodone going. Let us know if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day for the clot removal. You’ll be going to radiology in a few hours. Any questions before we start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is there a chance something could go wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Like any procedure, there are risks. One is that a small piece of clot could break off and go to the lungs. But the team is ready for that and will monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds scary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But it’s rare, and if it happens, it often resolves on its own. We won’t use blood thinners because of your history of stomach bleeds, but we’ll watch you carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. Johnson. You’re back from the procedure. It went well — they cleared the clot and opened up the graft. You have good blood flow now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember feeling short of breath for a bit… and some chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that happened. The radiologist thinks a small clot may have gone to your lung — a minor pulmonary embolism. But your oxygen recovered quickly, and you’re stable now. No treatment is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You were a bit groggy afterward from the pain meds, but you’re alert now. We’ll keep an eye on your oxygen and blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My feet still hurt, but not as bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your pain meds going, but we’ll be cautious so you don’t get too sleepy. Your neuropathy is chronic, so we’re not changing anything there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your dialysis went well this afternoon. Your graft is working, and we’ll remove the groin catheter soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We want to make sure your blood pressure stays stable. You had a drop last night — probably from fasting and dialysis — but it’s back to normal now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve always run a little low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and that’s okay as long as you feel fine. We’ll check one more dialysis session tomorrow, and if all looks good, you can go back to your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — your labs are stable, your graft is working, and your oxygen is 100% on your usual 2 liters. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my CPAP? I haven’t been using it at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting it. You have sleep apnea, and using CPAP helps your heart and oxygen levels. Your sleep specialist wants to see you for a mask fitting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But it’s uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with the sleep team to get it adjusted. It’s important, especially after what happened with your oxygen during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my heart medicine — diltiazem — is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s still prescribed. You’re not on blood thinners because of your past stomach bleeds, but the diltiazem helps control your rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll keep your insulin — glargine and the sliding scale. Your blood sugar is a bit high, but stable. We’ll leave adjustments to your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And when do I see the cardiologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have an appointment scheduled for next week. Also, don’t forget your sleep specialist. We’re sending instructions to your facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, doc.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. One last thing — weigh yourself every morning. If you gain more than three pounds, call your doctor. That could mean fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I remember from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And if you have trouble breathing on your usual oxygen, let someone know right away. Otherwise, you’re doing well and ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. Your graft has a good thrill and bruit — that means it’s working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can feel it pulsing now. Much better than before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That’s what we want. Keep an eye on it — if it ever stops pulsing or becomes painful, let your team know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your potassium is stable, and your kidney function is as expected for someone on dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more emergency dialysis, I hope.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not if we can help it. Keeping your graft healthy is key. That means no pressure on the arm and checking the site daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And keep taking your sevelamer with meals — it helps control your phosphorus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I remember that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, everything looks good. We’ll get the discharge papers ready. You should be on your way within a few hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll follow up with the specialists.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, Mr. Johnson.
